key_results: An ideal discrete-time differentiator has H(ω)=jω: magnitude proportional to |ω| and a +90° phase shift for positive frequency. First- and central-difference FIR approximations trade usable linear bandwidth, high-frequency noise gain, and delay; an antisymmetric length-(D+1) FIR differentiator has group delay D/2. [§7.1.1, Eqs. 7-2–7-7, Figs. 7-1–7-3]

Windowed narrowband differentiators (Hamming, Lanczos, and super-Lanczos variants) reduce high-frequency noise at the cost of a narrower accurate differentiation band and more multiplies. [§7.1.2, Fig. 7-4]

The wideband differentiator impulse response follows from the inverse Fourier transform of the ideal response; the practical coefficient expression in Eq. 7-15 supports arbitrary cutoff, odd or even tap counts, and nonnegative coefficient indexing. Parks–McClellan optimization becomes attractive for longer filters, while even-tap designs impose fractional-sample delay. [§§7.1.3–7.1.4, Eqs. 7-8–7-15]

Rectangular-, trapezoidal-, Simpson-, and Tick-rule digital integrators approximate the ideal 1/|ω| magnitude and −90° phase. Simpson and Tick are most accurate at low frequency, but their z=−1 poles amplify Nyquist-region noise; every listed integrator has a z=1 pole and therefore needs enough word width to tolerate accumulated DC bias. [§§7.2.1–7.2.5, Figs. 7-6–7-10]

For a known finite signal in additive white Gaussian noise, a matched filter maximizes output SNR. Its frequency response is the conjugated signal spectrum with a delay, and its N-sample digital impulse response is the time-reversed signal h(k)=x_s(N−1−k); consequently matched filtering is correlation. [§7.3.1, Eqs. 7-28–7-34]

Matched-filter detection requires a threshold: raising it reduces false alarms but increases missed detections. Direct convolution is natural for short templates, while FFT convolution may be more efficient once the template is roughly longer than 80 samples. [§§7.3.2–7.3.3, Figs. 7-12–7-13]

An interpolated FIR (IFIR) design expands a sparse model filter by replacing each unit delay with M delays, which compresses and repeats its frequency response; a shorter image-reject filter then removes the unwanted replicas. The expansion factor is chosen to minimize the combined model-plus-image-reject tap count subject to transition constraints. [§§7.4.1–7.4.3, Figs. 7-14–7-17]

IFIR efficiency depends on preserving the two sparse stages rather than convolving them into one ordinary FIR. Efficient implementations exploit stride-M addressing and folded linear-phase structures; the architecture trades extra state memory for far fewer multiplications. [§§7.4.4–7.4.5]

A frequency-sampling filter (FSF) cascades a comb, whose zeros are the Nth roots of unity, with resonators that cancel selected comb zeros. When only a few DFT frequency samples are nonzero, this realizes a narrowband FIR filter with far less arithmetic than a direct-form implementation. [§§7.5.1–7.5.2, Figs. 7-23–7-29]

Finite coefficient precision can push nominal unit-circle resonator poles outside the unit circle. Moving poles and matching zeros to radius r<1 guarantees stability; a fixed-point-friendly choice is r=1−2^(−B), chosen as close to one as the word format permits. [§7.5.3, Figs. 7-30–7-32]

The Type-IV real-valued FSF is the preferred architecture in this treatment: it is guaranteed stable, uses real coefficients, has highly linear phase, supports highpass designs, and admits transition-band coefficients that materially improve ripple and stopband attenuation. [§§7.5.4–7.5.10]

The source’s design boundary is empirical: Type-IV FSFs are often more efficient than Parks–McClellan FIR filters when the passband is below about f_s/5 and the transition width is below about f_s/8. [§§7.5.11–7.5.15, Fig. 7-48]

A quadrature signal is a two-dimensional complex signal with mutually orthogonal in-phase and quadrature components. Multiplication by j rotates a complex sample 90° counterclockwise and multiplication by −j rotates it clockwise. [§§8.1–8.2, Figs. 8-1–8-4]

Euler’s identity represents a real cosine or sine as the sum or difference of oppositely rotating complex exponentials. This phasor representation supplies the link between time-domain sinusoids, complex-plane rotation, and spectral impulses. [§8.3, Eqs. 8-7–8-14, Figs. 8-5–8-11]

Negative frequency denotes clockwise complex-plane rotation under the book’s convention. Real signals have conjugate-symmetric spectra, whereas an analytic complex signal can contain only positive-frequency content. [§§8.4–8.6, Figs. 8-12–8-15]

Complex multiplication by exp(+j2πf_ot) shifts a spectrum upward by f_o; the negative-exponent mixer shifts it downward. The spectral-circle view makes alias wraparound at ±f_s/2 explicit. [§§8.6–8.7, Figs. 8-16–8-20]

Quadrature down-conversion uses coherent cosine and sine mixers to form I and Q baseband sequences. Compared with a single real high-rate path it can halve the required converter rate, reduce power, widen processable bandwidth, and make instantaneous magnitude and phase directly available. [§8.8, Figs. 8-18–8-21]

Digitizing before quadrature mixing removes one A/D converter and avoids analog I/Q phase mismatch. At f_c=f_s/4 the oscillator sequences contain only 0 and ±1, so the mixer needs no general multipliers. [§8.9, Figs. 8-22–8-24]
The Hilbert transform applies −j to positive frequencies and +j to negative frequencies, producing a 90° phase shift without changing magnitude. [§9.1, Figs. 9-2–9-3]

The analytic signal x_c=x_r+jH{x_r} cancels the negative-frequency half of a real signal’s spectrum and doubles its positive-frequency half. Its magnitude, angle, and angle derivative provide envelope, instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency. [§9.2, Figs. 9-4–9-8]
The ideal discrete Hilbert-transform impulse response is odd and antisymmetric, is zero at even indices, and decays at odd indices as 1, 1/3, 1/5, …. [§9.3, Fig. 9-9]

Odd-tap Type-III FIR Hilbert transformers have zeros at DC and Nyquist and integer group delay; even-tap Type-IV designs retain Nyquist response but require fractional-sample delay. Windowing the truncated ideal impulse response reduces Gibbs ripple while narrowing the useful band. [§9.4.1, Figs. 9-10–9-13]

A time-domain analytic-signal generator must delay the real path by the Hilbert FIR group delay before pairing it with the quadrature output. Antisymmetric coefficient conventions also require attention to coefficient reversal in convolution. [§9.4.1, Fig. 9-12]

For even-length blocks, an FFT-domain analytic-signal construction doubles positive-frequency bins, zeros negative-frequency bins, leaves DC and the Nyquist endpoint with their required half weighting, and inverse-transforms. It is often the best high-performance block method and avoids a separate path-alignment delay. [§9.4.2, Fig. 9-14]

A complex bandpass FIR can generate I/Q outputs with useful filtering, but its real output need not equal the original input; the standard Hilbert pair preserves the input but adds no band selection. The DFT method is the full-band block-processing alternative. [§§9.5–9.6, Figs. 9-15–9-17]

Decimation by M is anti-alias lowpass filtering followed by retaining every Mth sample, giving f_s,new=f_s,old/M. Implementations should avoid computing outputs that will be discarded. [§10.1, Figs. 10-1–10-3]

Two-stage decimation M=M_1M_2 can reduce the total filter order dramatically, typically placing the larger factor first. In the 400 kHz-to-4 kHz, 60 dB example, a single-stage estimate is 2727 taps, whereas near-optimal M_1=25 and M_2=4 requires only a few hundred. [§§10.2.1–10.2.3, Fig. 10-4]

Downsampling is not time invariant. It leaves retained sample amplitudes unchanged, while normalized discrete-frequency spectral magnitudes scale by 1/M and shifted spectral copies can alias. [§§10.3.1–10.3.2, Figs. 10-5–10.8]

Interpolation by L inserts L−1 zeros between input samples and then lowpass filters the resulting images. To preserve constant-signal amplitude, the interpolation filter must have DC gain L. [§§10.4–10.5, Figs. 10-9–10-14]

Rational sample-rate conversion by L/M normally interpolates first, applies one shared lowpass filter, and then decimates, with the passband limited by the smaller input/output Nyquist band. [§§10.6, 10.11, Figs. 10-15 and 10-24]

Polyphase decomposition divides a prototype into subfilters and, using the noble identities, moves filtering to the low-rate side of a sampler. This eliminates multiplies by inserted zeros and computations for discarded outputs; an M-fold decimator reduces multiplication rate by approximately M. [§§10.7, 10.9–10.11, Figs. 10-18–10-24]

Half-band FIR filters have every other coefficient zero except the center coefficient, making them especially efficient for powers-of-two conversion. In cascaded interpolation the later, higher-rate stages can use progressively fewer taps; tiny theoretical zero coefficients should be forced to exact zero in implementation. [§10.12, Figs. 10-25–10-30]

A CIC filter is a cascade of integrators and combs equivalent to repeated moving-average filters. It uses only additions and subtractions, has linear phase and sinc-like magnitude, and is unconditionally stable when its unit coefficients are represented exactly. Its DC gain is D^Q for differential delay D and order Q. [§§10.14.1–10.14.3, Figs. 10-33–10-37]

For CIC decimation, integrators operate before the downsampler and combs after it; interpolation reverses that order, keeping comb computation at the low rate. Two’s-complement internal wraparound is harmless if register widths and the final comb difference satisfy the stated gain bound. [§10.14.4, Figs. 10-38–10-40]

A short FIR compensation filter can approximate the inverse of the CIC passband droop. Compensation should be confined to roughly the first quarter of the first CIC null to avoid excessive high-frequency noise amplification. [§10.14.5, Figs. 10-41–10-43]

Coherent averaging requires sample/phase synchronization and preserves a repeatable signal while uncorrelated zero-mean noise decreases: variance falls as 1/N, standard deviation as 1/√N, and SNR improves by 10log10(N) dB. [§11.1, Eqs. 11-1–11-14, Figs. 11-1–11-3]

Incoherent averaging of magnitude or power spectra reduces display variance and measurement fluctuation, but it does not lower the average noise floor or improve the underlying signal-to-noise ratio. [§11.2, Fig. 11-4]

Averaging several shorter FFT magnitudes can be cheaper and more display-stable than one long transform but sacrifices frequency resolution. Coherent complex-bin averaging is meaningful only when records are synchronized to repeatable periodic content. [§11.3, Figs. 11-5–11-7]
Circular phase data must be averaged as complex vectors, not as scalar angles; angles near +π and −π otherwise average spuriously near zero. [§11.4, Fig. 11-8]

An N-point moving average is an FIR lowpass with sinc-like magnitude and equally spaced unit-circle zeros. Its recursive form produces the same response with two additions per output regardless of N, and white-noise variance is reduced by N. [§11.5, Figs. 11-9–11-11]

The exponential averager y(n)=αx(n)+(1−α)y(n−1) has one pole at z=1−α. Smaller α gives stronger smoothing but slower response; its white-noise variance-reduction factor is (2−α)/α, so α=2/(R+1) targets reduction R and α≈2/(N+1) roughly matches an N-point moving average. [§§11.6.1–11.6.2, Figs. 11-12–11-14]

For a signed fixed-point word with one sign bit and b magnitude bits, dynamic range is approximately 6.02b dB—the familiar 6 dB per bit rule. Binary-point placement trades representable range against resolution without changing the underlying two’s-complement adder or multiplier behavior. [§§12.1.6–12.2, Eq. 12-6]

A b-bit ideal A/D converter with peak range ±V_p has quantization step q=2V_p/2^b. Under the uniform, stationary, signal-uncorrelated error model, quantization error lies in ±q/2 with variance q²/12. [§12.3.1, Eqs. 12-7–12-10, Figs. 12-1–12-3]

Ideal A/D SNR is 6.02b+4.77+20log10(LF) dB for loading factor LF=V_rms/V_p; a full-scale sine gives 6.02b+1.76 dB. Practical design needs headroom and nonideal converters often deliver 3–6 dB less; useful converter SNR should be only about 6 dB above the analog signal’s SNR. [§12.3.1, Eqs. 12-11–12-16, Fig. 12-4]

The sum of m unsigned b-bit values can require b+ceil(log2 m) bits. Two’s-complement additions may wrap at intermediate stages yet still yield the correct final sum when the true final value is representable; overflow is detected when carry into and out of the sign bit differ. [§12.3.2, Fig. 12-5]

FFT butterflies can grow a component by more than a factor of two in one stage, and feedback networks need accumulator width for their DC gain: at least the input width plus ceil(log2 G) bits for gain G. [§12.3.2, Eqs. 12-17–12-22, Fig. 12-6]

Truncation has error over [−q,0), mean −q/2, and variance q²/12, so it introduces DC bias. Rounding has error bounded by ±q/2, zero ideal mean, and variance q²/12; round-to-even removes the slight upward tie bias of ordinary round-to-nearest. [§§12.3.3–12.3.4, Eqs. 12-23–12-26, Figs. 12-7–12-9]
Preserve full precision through a chain of arithmetic and round or truncate only once, at the final operation, to minimize accumulated quantization error. [§12.3.4]

A floating-point value is n=m·2^e, with word bits divided between exponent range and mantissa precision. Normalization places the leading one at a known location, allowing formats such as IEEE P754 to omit it as a hidden bit. [§12.4, Eqs. 12-27–12-34, Table 12-6]

Block floating point normalizes a whole array to one shared exponent, then performs fixed-point arithmetic; when a stage overflows, all words shift right and the shared exponent increments. It extends fixed-point range with less hardware than full floating point, but cannot match full floating-point performance. [§12.5]
pedagogy: Engineering-intuition-first treatment with informal derivations rather than theorem-proof formalism. Lyons repeatedly moves among an equation, a block diagram, pole-zero or spectral picture, and a concrete implementation consequence; many sections compare several structures by accuracy, multiply/add count, delay, memory, numerical stability, or noise behavior. Worked designs use explicit sample rates, transition bands, attenuation targets, tap estimates, and hardware constraints. End-of-chapter problem sets are substantial and varied: derivations and proofs, hand-drawn spectra, coefficient calculations, debugging of plausible but wrong systems, algorithm/block-diagram design, and realistic vendor-part or communications examples. The shard assumes prior command of discrete sequences, convolution, FIR/IIR filters, DFT/FFT, z-transforms, decibels, and elementary probability/statistics; Chapter 8 refreshes complex arithmetic before Chapters 8–9 rely heavily on it, while Chapters 11–12 point back to the statistics appendix. The style is conversational and memorable, with side remarks and analogies used to surface engineering pitfalls.

gems: A nine-sample matched-filter template is hidden twice in strong random noise; the output correlation peaks recover both events and make threshold tradeoffs concrete. [§7.3.2, Figs. 7-12–7-13]
IFIR design example: a conventional 137-tap lowpass becomes 45 model taps plus 25 image-reject taps—70 total, about a 49% reduction. [§7.4.5]

A more demanding IFIR example (f_pass=0.02f_s, transition 0.01f_s, 50 dB) uses M=7 and 33+27=60 taps instead of roughly 240, a 75% reduction; the text notes savings can approach 90% for under 10% extra memory. [§7.4.5]

The six-section N=62 Type-IV FSF example meets 0.05f_s cutoff, 0.095f_s stopband start, ≤0.3 dB ripple, and ≥65 dB attenuation with 17 multiplies and 19 adds, versus 30 multiplies and 59 adds for a folded 60-tap Parks–McClellan FIR. [§7.5.12, Figs. 7-46–7-47]
The warning that theory and practice differ because in theory they do not is deployed exactly where finite precision threatens nominally perfect FSF pole-zero cancellation. [§7.5.3]

A complexity-only comparison is likened to modern swimwear: what it shows matters, and what it omits is vital—an invitation to include memory, control, and numeric behavior alongside multiply counts. [§7.5.11, Fig. 7-45]

Euler’s identity is called the Rosetta Stone of quadrature signal processing, then made physical as a corkscrew trajectory whose projections are cosine and sine and whose XY oscilloscope trace is a circle. [§8.3, Figs. 8-5–8-8]

A 50 MHz band can be bandpass-sampled at 40 MHz and shifted digitally by f_s/4=10 MHz; the I/Q local-oscillator sequences are only 1, 0, −1, 0 and 0, −1, 0, 1, eliminating general multipliers. [§8.9, Figs. 8-22–8-24]

The analytic signal shifts a 25 kHz real signal cleanly to 20 kHz by multiplication with exp(−j2π·5000t), avoiding the difficult image-rejection filter that a real mixer would require. [§9.2, Fig. 9-8]

The 400 kHz-to-4 kHz decimator with a 0–1.8 kHz retained band and 60 dB rejection is estimated at 2727 taps as one stage; factoring 100 as 25×4 cuts the design to a few hundred taps. [§10.2.2, Fig. 10-4]
CIC filters are described as ‘lean, mean, fat-free filtering machines’: add/subtract-only structures that turn a severe multirate task into low-rate comb work plus high-rate accumulators. [§10.14]

The CIC two’s-complement example makes intentional overflow tangible: an integrator can wrap repeatedly, yet modulo arithmetic lets the downstream comb recover the correct result when word width meets the output bound. [§10.14.4, Fig. 10-40]
A pulse of amplitude 2.5 is visually lost in one noisy record, begins to emerge after 32 coherent averages, and is unmistakable after 256. [§11.1, Figs. 11-1–11-3]

The chapter punctures a common misconception: averaging 10 or 100 FFT magnitudes makes the spectrum steadier but does not improve the actual signal-to-noise ratio or lower the mean noise floor. [§11.2, Fig. 11-4]
A charge-card magnetic-stripe reader motivates exponential averaging as a practical compromise between smoothing and the need to respond before the card has already passed the sensor. [§11.6.3]

The dynamic exponential averager starts with a large α for fast acquisition and decreases it over time for quiet steady-state estimates, turning an apparent smoothing-versus-response tradeoff into a scheduling problem. [§11.6.3]

The 64-bit counter aside notes that incrementing once per second since the beginning of the universe would still leave its four most significant bits zero—a memorable scale for 2^64. [§12.2, footnote to Eq. 12-6]
The 8-bit A/D example turns one LSB into 7.81 mV over a ±1 V range, then follows the resulting ±3.905 mV error from a time-domain staircase into broadband DFT noise. [§12.3.1, Figs. 12-1–12-2]

A full-scale ideal 8-bit converter reaches only 49.9 dB SNR, so digitizing a 55 dB analog signal loses information; a 10-bit ideal converter’s roughly 62 dB ceiling is the safer match. [§12.3.1, discussion after Eq. 12-15]

The overflow section escalates from an eight-digit calculator turning 99,999,999+1 into 1 to an FFT butterfly whose real or imaginary component can more than double in one stage. [§12.3.2, Eqs. 12-17–12-21]
Dividing 31 by 16 via a four-bit right shift returns 1 instead of 1.9375—roughly 50% error—making truncation’s dependence on discarded bits and residual magnitude painfully concrete. [§12.3.3]
Block floating point is presented as a marriage: an FFT block shares one exponent, behaves like fixed point until overflow, then shifts every word and increments the shared exponent. [§12.5]
